request.lesson: A test that pins a security control by substring-matching the source cannot detect that control's removal. Two gates here asserted things like 'build_opener(_NoRedirect)' appearing in the source text; deleting the method the control actually lives in left both fully green while the behaviour was gone -- in one case a bearer JWT would have been forwarded across an origin change. The substring survives the deletion because it names where the control is CALLED, not what it DOES. Pin a control by observing the production path instead: spy the collaborator (monkeypatch the opener factory, the subprocess runner, the request builder), invoke the real entry point, and assert on what it was handed. Then verify the pin by deleting the control and confirming the test goes red -- an unmutated assertion is an unverified one. The same reasoning applies to scope rather than behaviour: a gate whose scanned file set can collapse to zero while still exiting 0 is silent when it works and silent when it is broken.

A negative-path assertion can pass for the wrong reason. A case asserting "invalid input is rejected" only means anything if the code under test is the only thing that can reject it. Stub the collaborators around the positive case but not the negative one, and the real collaborator raises the same exception type for an unrelated reason: the assertion is green, the control is absent, and nothing says so. Observed here on a case asserting that a builder validates its subject argument -- it was catching the error from an unstubbed network read, and deleting the validation left the suite green. Two rules follow. Stub every collaborator around the negative case, not only the positive one. Then delete the control and re-run: if the suite does not go red, the assertion is not testing what its name says. The same reasoning covers shell gates in CI. `pip install ""` exits 0 with no output, and a command substitution that fails inside a run block does not fail the step unless it sits in an assignment under set -e, so a provisioning step can install nothing and stay green while the gate it exists to enable silently no-ops.

A reported case count is not coverage, and an assertion that cannot fail is worse than a missing one because it reports confidence. Four shapes showed up in one review of otherwise careful test code: a helper that pre-filtered the very field the assertion then checked, so attribution could not fail for any input; two string literals defined in the test file compared to each other while the subject was never run; `assert X or <non-empty constant>`; and `len(dict) == len(set(dict))`, which is true by construction. Each looked like coverage and cost maintenance. Two habits catch them cheaply: derive coverage mechanically rather than counting cases (an AST sweep for the subject's finding-emission sites, driven with a recording collector, found four unexercised branches behind a growing case count), and mutation-test any assertion you rely on — weaken the subject and confirm the test reds.

When an exception class gates a DESTRUCTIVE action, give the reader a typed hierarchy rather than matching on the message. loop-engine decided whether to delete events.pending — a durable audit record — by testing str(exc) against a hand-listed set of message fragments, duplicated at two call sites. The list had already fallen behind the reader it mirrored: it omitted the non-finite-number message, so a NaN or 1e400 in events.pending was never recognised as invalid content and the file was retained forever, re-warning on every transition. The fix is ManagedContentError(ValueError) raised at the content sites plus one isinstance-based helper: 'the bytes are unusable' and 'the read failed' are different facts, and only the first may authorise a delete. Subclassing ValueError kept every existing except clause working unchanged.

A reachability or call-graph assertion can be vacuous in a way its own vacuity guard misses. The AC21 test walked lint-spec-status.py from the guard-path entry symbols and asserted no spawn was reachable, plus that the spawning functions were disjoint from the reachable set. Both are trivially true when the walk resolves nothing — and it resolved nothing, because those entry symbols call no other same-module function. Patching reachable_from to return set() left it green, while workspace.toml cited the assertion by name as the reason four unbounded git calls stayed unbounded. An empty-set assertion needs a POSITIVE CONTROL: a root known to reach the thing, asserted to reach it. Proving the walker traverses is a different claim from proving the target set is empty.

friction.summary: Two spec-stage review rounds before the criterion form was identified as the cause.

request.lesson: An acceptance criterion that asserts a property of the code's character instead of naming an input and an observable is unfalsifiable, and it generates review churn that compounds. Phrasings like "writability is a filesystem fact", "exclusion is structural", "the record is revalidated in full", or "no module reads the clock" give a reviewer nothing to test, so the reviewer correctly answers "names no mechanism"; the author then adds prose, and the prose becomes the next round's surface. Measured on one spec-stage loop: round one produced 36 findings across two reviewers, and round two produced 43 more of which 33 were caused by round one's own remedies. Write each criterion as: given this concrete input, this exact observable - a published refusal code, a field value, a byte comparison, or an enumerated symbol set over an enumerated path. Naming a refusal code in a criterion is an outcome, not leaked mechanism; the line is observable-versus-implementation, not detail-versus-prose. Rewriting on that rule cut median criterion length from 71 words to 38, removed every compound criterion, and independently covered four of the five blockers the next adjudication sustained.
